corrections.why: 1798 is the date of Dearborn's contract (LighthouseFriends) and of the 1937 Lighthouse Service article's 'constructed'; the first tower was lit in 1803 (Park Service: October 1803) and the present tower on December 16, 1870.

The standing tower is brick, begun October 1868 and lit December 16, 1870; the 1802/1803 sandstone tower was demolished in 1871. Heights differ by source: 60.5 m (Park Service), 63 m from the base of the foundation (Cloyd).

1871 is when the old 1803 tower was demolished, not when the light ended; no source read says the present light was discontinued in 1893 (the light moved to a skeleton tower in 1935/36 and returned to the tower on January 23, 1950). 1893 may belong to another structure, such as the beacon.
The Park Service gives the official range as 24 nautical miles; the record's 14 nm may be a Light List figure for a different configuration. Needs a Light List check.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Several towers and several 'firsts': contract 1798, first tower finished late 1802, lit 1803, raised and given a Fresnel lens 1853-54, present tower built 1868-70 and lit December 16, 1870.

Sources give 193 ft (1937 bulletin), 198.49 ft (Park Service, foundation to pinnacle), 63 m from the foundation (Cloyd) and 208 ft (LighthouseFriends); the differences are mostly where each measures from.

notes_for_editor: Rich public sources for the 1870 tower, the Civil War lens, the 1930s retreat and the 1999 move; thin for individual keepers (roster only, from the USLHS archive, whose lines are quoted exactly). The local corpus holds the Light-House Board reports only from 1891, so the 1850s and 1860s Board reports (the 1851 inspector quotes, the lens removal, the 1868-70 construction) are cited through LighthouseFriends, Duffus and the Park Service as second-hand. The Civil War lens account rests mainly on Kevin Duffus (Island Free Press); LighthouseFriends says in one paragraph both that the old tower's lens went to Pigeon Point and that the 1870 lens was the original, so the Pigeon Point claim is reported but not endorsed. Conflicts stated in the story: authorization 1794/1797; first tower dates 1798/1802/1803; lighting day 16 Dec vs 1 Dec 1870; height; foundation depth (about 4, 6 or 9 feet); abandonment 1935 vs May 13, 1936; transfer to NPS 1936 vs Nov 9, 1937; lightship sunk 1918 No. 71 (Commissioner) vs No. 69 (Park Service). Roster names are from USLHS (NARA registers via Kraig Anderson) and match LighthouseFriends's list exactly; the 'Contractor' entries (Charles Cluskey, John McComb Jr.) have no dates and were left out of the roster. Unaka Jennette's two Diamond Shoals lightship stints are linked to the lightship station record on LighthouseFriends's say-so. Page numbers for the Light-House Board volumes are scan pages; printed pages not confirmed. No newspapers were read (a Chronicling America search on 'Hatteras' returned only shipping notes). The Park Service's visitor page says the tower is closed to climbing for 2026 for restoration; check before publishing. Fact-check 2026-10-22: Stetson's title differs by source (superintendent of construction in LighthouseFriends and the Simpson letter; foreman in the Park Service and Cloyd); foundation depth now also gives the Park Service's 7.5 ft. Cloyd's employer is not stated in the paper, so the story calls him an engineer only. Light-House Board page numbers remain scan pages.
